steps: Here billing clerk forty-seven signs in through single sign-on, with billing scope, and asks the assistant about customer C seventy-seven.
First, the wrong way. The C R M key sits in the system prompt, so Claude and every trace can see it, and it can leak through logs or prompt injection.
Now your design. The server sends only the question and the tools, with no secret in context, and Claude asks for lookup customer, C seventy-seven.
At execution time, the handler pulls the C R M A P I key from Key Vault, on the server side. It is used in the request header, then discarded.
The call also carries the clerk's billing-scoped token, so role-based access control runs before data returns. Only billing documents come back, since V I P notes need V I P support access.
Next, Claude gets the tool result and writes the answer about C seventy-seven. It never held the key at all.
Finally, the clerk sees only billing-scoped data, and the audit log records that clerk forty-seven viewed customer C seventy-seven. Secrets stay server-side, and access stays in scope.
